idiom_name: first-class predicate functions with filter/some/every; closures for parameterized rules
implementation_notes: A rule is simply a function (candidate) => boolean; composition is either an ordinary expression inside a new arrow function or a two-line combinator (`const and = (...rules) => c => rules.every(r => r(c))`), and Array.prototype.filter/some/every consume it directly. Parameterized rules are factories returning a closure (`const overdue = days => inv => Date.now() - inv.dueDate > days * 864e5`). The classic object form - a class with isSatisfiedBy - is justified when the rule must carry metadata for logging or error messages, be serialized, or be rendered into a query by the data layer; otherwise it adds nothing over a named function, which is JavaScript's built-in realization of the pattern.
pitfalls: filter() coerces the result to truthiness, so a rule returning undefined, 0 or an object silently changes the selection; keep predicates strictly boolean.
A closure over a mutated variable (a request object, an accumulator) makes the rule stateful and order-dependent; capture the values the rule needs.
Nothing distinguishes a specification from a plain callback at runtime: a rule that throws or returns a Promise only fails at the call site, so add TypeScript/JSDoc types or validate inputs.
Filtering in memory means client-side evaluation; for large data sets the rule must also exist as a query in the data layer, which is a second definition that can drift.
